chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Emerging Market Crises of the 1990s

lessons.title: Russia's 1998 Default and the Fall of LTCM

body.text: A trade that has worked every day for four years can still be the most dangerous trade in the world, if it is leveraged 25 times and everyone rushes for the same exit at once.

children.text: On 23 September 1998, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought together the biggest creditors of a single hedge fund, run by star bond traders and two Nobel Prize winners. Five weeks earlier, a default in Moscow had set off a chain reaction the fund's models had treated as almost impossible. That day, 14 banks and brokerage firms agreed to put in $3.6 billion to keep it from collapsing.

This lesson tells two linked stories: how Russia defaulted on its own rouble debt, and how that default nearly brought down Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), a fund whose failure the Fed feared could freeze global markets.

stats.label: Private rescue brokered by the NY Fed
stats.context: From 14 banks and brokers, for 90% of the fund

body.caption: Two crises on the five-stage map

children.text: Russia: A Government Hooked on Short-Term Debt
After the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia struggled to collect taxes and ran large budget deficits. To fund them, it sold short-term rouble treasury bills called
GKOs
. By 1998, the government was paying enormous yields to keep rolling them over, and foreign investors had piled in, attracted by returns that looked too good to miss while the rouble was held stable.

markDefs.definition: Russian government short-term, rouble-denominated treasury bills issued in the 1990s. By 1998 they paid extremely high yields and had to be constantly rolled over.

children.text: The Asian crisis made investors nervous about every emerging market, and a slump in oil and commodity prices cut Russia's export earnings. An IMF-led package in July 1998, and a swap of some GKOs into longer-term dollar bonds, bought only weeks.

On 17 August 1998, the government gave up on all three fronts at once. It abandoned its defence of the rouble, defaulted on its domestic GKO debt, and imposed a 90-day moratorium on commercial foreign debt payments. GKO yields shot above 100%, and by 9 September the rouble had fallen from 6.29 to 21 per dollar.

body.text: Notice what was unusual. Russia defaulted on debt in its own currency, which a government can in theory always repay by printing money. It chose default over printing because printing enough roubles would have unleashed hyperinflation. "They can always print" is not the same as "they will always pay".

body.title: The High-Yield Trap
body.question: A foreign investor put $1 million into GKOs yielding 50% a year when the rouble was 6.29 per dollar. Suppose, optimistically, that Russia paid in full a year later, but the rouble was then 21 per dollar. Roughly what was the investor's return in dollars?
body.explanation: $1 million bought 6.29 million roubles. At 50%, that grows to 9.435 million roubles. Converted back at 21 per dollar, that is about $449,000, a loss of about 55% in dollars. A huge local yield is worthless if the currency falls further. In reality it was worse, because Russia did not pay GKO holders in full.

children.text: LTCM: Genius, Leverage and a Crowded Exit

Long-Term Capital Management was founded in February 1994 by John Meriwether, a former vice chairman of Salomon Brothers. Its partners included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the Nobel Prize in economics in 1997 for their work on pricing options. After fees, the fund returned 43% in 1995 and 41% in 1996, then 17% in 1997.
Its core strategy was the
convergence trade

. A simple example: two almost identical US government bonds, one newly issued and heavily traded, one slightly older and less traded. The older one usually yields a little more. LTCM would buy the cheaper older bond and sell the pricier newer one, profiting as the gap closed.

markDefs.definition: Buying one security and selling a closely related one when their prices have drifted unusually far apart, betting the gap will narrow back to normal. Profits per trade are small, so they are usually magnified with heavy leverage.

children.text: The profit on each trade was tiny, so LTCM used enormous leverage. In early 1998 it held about $125 billion of assets on roughly $4.7 billion of capital, plus derivatives with a notional value of more than $1.25 trillion.

body.caption: The same leverage formula from Chapter 1, Lesson 2: the percentage fall in assets that erases all capital.

body.title: How Thin Was LTCM's Cushion?
body.prompt: LTCM held about $125 billion of assets on about $4.7 billion of capital. By what percentage would the value of its assets need to fall, net of its hedges, to wipe out all its capital? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Wipeout point = $4.7 billion ÷ $125 billion × 100 = 3.76%, or about 3.8%. That is only slightly more than Lehman Brothers' cushion of about 3.3% in 2007. LTCM believed its positions were hedged, so a loss that large seemed near impossible. It happened anyway.

children.text: Why the Hedges Failed: Flight to Quality

LTCM's trades assumed that unusual price gaps between similar securities would narrow. After Russia's default, investors everywhere panicked and dumped anything risky or hard to sell, piling into the safest, most easily traded assets they could find. This is a
flight to quality

markDefs.definition: A rush by investors out of riskier or less liquid assets into the safest and most liquid ones, such as newly issued US government bonds, during periods of fear.

children.text: That meant the expensive, easy-to-trade bonds LTCM had sold got even more expensive, while the cheaper, harder-to-trade bonds it had bought got even cheaper. The gaps widened, on hundreds of trades at once, in markets around the world.

body.title: What LTCM's models assumed vs what happened in August 1998

columns.label: The models assumed
points: Price gaps between similar securities eventually return to normal
Trades in different countries and markets are largely unrelated
Positions can be adjusted or sold whenever needed
Past price patterns are a good guide to future risk

columns.label: What actually happened
points: Gaps widened sharply as investors fled to safety
Almost every trade lost money at the same time, because the same panic drove them all
Other traders knew LTCM's positions and would not buy them except at fire sale prices
A default by a major government created conditions the historical data had never shown

body.title: Name the Stampede
body.textWithBlank: When frightened investors sell risky assets and rush into the safest government bonds, it is called a flight to ___.
body.explanation: A flight to quality, sometimes called a flight to safety. It is the single biggest threat to any strategy that is long cheap, risky assets and short expensive, safe ones, however well hedged it looks in normal times.

body.text: LTCM was right that many of those price gaps would eventually close. But being right eventually is worthless when you are leveraged 25 times and your lenders want more collateral now. Leverage turns a correct idea with bad timing into a failure.

body.title: Go deeper: what the Fed feared if LTCM was left to fail

children.text: LTCM was not a bank, and no depositor would have lost money if it failed. The Fed's concern was the fund's place at the centre of a web of trades.
Its counterparties, the biggest banks on Wall Street and in Europe, would all rush to seize and sell the collateral they held at the same moment.
Dumping about $125 billion of positions into markets that were already frozen would crash prices for everyone holding similar securities, spreading the losses far beyond LTCM.
Banks hit by those losses might pull back from lending to each other and to businesses, turning a hedge fund failure into a credit crunch.

This is the fire sale channel of contagion from Chapter 1. The rescue avoided a disorderly dumping of positions. The trade-off, which critics raised at the time, was moral hazard: if large, interconnected funds can expect help, they may take even bigger risks next time. That same argument returns in 2008.
India in 1998: A Different Kind of Borrowing

India faced its own pressure in 1998. The Pokhran-II nuclear tests in May brought international sanctions and a credit rating downgrade, just as emerging markets were being shunned after Asia and Russia. Instead of relying on hot money, India turned to a loyal source of dollars: its diaspora.

body.label: Resurgent India Bonds, August 1998
body.context: SBI's scheme, open from 5 August 1998, raised a little over $4.2 billion in under a month, paying 7.75% in US dollars, well above US Treasury yields at the time. It came in the same month Russia defaulted, a striking contrast in how two countries under pressure found dollars.

children.text: The lesson India drew was the same one from 1991: who you borrow from matters as much as how much. Diaspora investors with long-term ties to the country were far less likely to flee at the first sign of trouble than portfolio money chasing yield. India would use the same idea again in 2013, which you will see in Chapter 4.

body.title: The Fund That Never Has a Bad Month
body.scenario: A wealth manager pitches you a leveraged "market-neutral" strategy run through a Category III Alternative Investment Fund. It has returned 16% to 18% a year for five years with almost no down months. The manager explains that it buys slightly underpriced corporate bonds and hedges by selling closely related, more liquid instruments, using borrowed money to magnify the small price gaps. "We are hedged, so market direction does not matter," they say.
body.prompt: Using what happened to LTCM, what questions would you ask before investing, and what kind of event would hurt this strategy most?
body.modelAnswer: The questions: first, how much leverage does the strategy use, and what is its wipeout point? A small cushion like LTCM's 3.8% means a modest, unexpected move can be fatal. Note that SEBI limits leverage for Category III AIFs, so ask how the fund complies and what its maximum is. Second, what happens if the gaps widen instead of narrowing, and how long can the fund survive that? Ask for its worst drawdown and its stress test assumptions. Third, how liquid are the bonds it holds, and could it sell them in a panic without taking huge losses? Fourth, who are its lenders, and can they demand more collateral at short notice? Fifth, are its many trades really independent, or would one market-wide shock hit all of them together? The event that would hurt most is a flight to quality: a sudden panic, like a major default, where investors dump less liquid corporate bonds and rush into the most liquid instruments. That widens exactly the gap the strategy is betting will narrow, at the moment lenders are most likely to demand collateral. Five years of smooth returns tell you the strategy works in calm markets. They tell you almost nothing about how it behaves in a panic.

body.title: Red Flags from 1998, for Any High-Yield or "Hedged" Investment
steps: Is the headline yield far above what similar safe instruments pay? Ask what risk you are being paid for.
Is the return earned in a currency that could fall against the one you spend in?
Does the strategy use leverage, and do you know how small a loss would wipe out its capital?
Does "hedged" rely on normal relationships between prices holding during a crisis?
Could the assets be sold quickly in a panic without large losses?
Is a long record of smooth returns being used as proof that the strategy is safe?

points: Russia funded chronic deficits with short-term rouble GKOs and, on 17 August 1998, devalued, defaulted on them and froze commercial foreign debt payments
The rouble fell from 6.29 to 21 per dollar in under four weeks, so even very high GKO yields turned into large dollar losses
LTCM held about $125 billion of assets on $4.7 billion of capital, a wipeout point below 4%, betting that price gaps between similar securities would narrow
The flight to quality after Russia's default widened those gaps across all its trades at once, and LTCM lost $4.6 billion in less than four months
The New York Fed brokered a $3.6 billion private rescue to avoid a fire sale, while India raised about $4.2 billion from its diaspora through Resurgent India Bonds
